bt67yj-k39888-d1e106.summary: Rubric heading for section 5, announcing the topic: where God was before the world was created.

bt67yj-k39888-d1e113.summary: The paragraph poses the question of where God was or dwelt before the creation of the world, and reports that some answer he was then in 'imaginary spaces,' since even now he is in such spaces outside the world; it announces that several reasons will be given to persuade that God must be granted to exist in such imaginary places or spaces.
claims: Some hold that before creation God existed in 'imaginary spaces,' just as he is now said to be in such spaces beyond the actual world.

bt67yj-k39888-d1e131.summary: First argument for God's presence in imaginary spaces: if God is not outside the world, it would follow that he is in the world definitively, the way the soul is in the body — present in the world such that he is not elsewhere — which is precisely what 'definitive' presence in a place means.
claims: If God were not outside the world, he would be in the world only definitively, like the soul in the body, which seems unfitting for God.

bt67yj-k39888-d1e145.summary: Second argument: an angel is said to be in a place when its operative power is applied to that place such that, without any change in itself, it could operate there, even if it does not actually do so; but God can, without change in himself, operate and produce something in imaginary spaces outside the world; therefore he is in those spaces.
claims: By analogy with the angelic criterion for presence (capacity to operate without self-change), since God could act in imaginary spaces without being changed, God is in those spaces.

bt67yj-k39888-d1e163.summary: Third argument: if the whole universe were moved to another place, God would not be moved, not even accidentally, the way the soul is moved by the motion of the body; therefore God must already have been in the place to which the universe is supposed to move, since if he were not there, he would be moved accidentally to it by the motion of the universe while simultaneously leaving his prior place — which is inadmissible.
claims: God's immunity to even accidental motion when the universe hypothetically moves implies he must already be present in whatever place the universe would move to.
concepts: thought experiment about moving the universe

bt67yj-k39888-d1e189.summary: Fourth argument: God existed before all real time; therefore he is outside all real place.
claims: Since God is prior to all real time, he is likewise outside all real place — an inferred parallel between time and place.

bt67yj-k39888-d1e198.summary: Fifth argument, from Scripture: 3 Kings 8 ('heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain you') and Job 11 (God is higher than heaven, deeper than hell, longer than earth, broader than sea) are read figuratively as signifying that God is outside the whole universe, which is enclosed by heaven as its outermost body; the same point is found in liturgical texts addressed to the Virgin, who contained the one whom the heavens and the whole world could not contain.
claims: Scriptural and liturgical texts describing God's transcendence of heaven and the cosmos are cited as evidence that God exists outside the whole universe in some space beyond it.
concepts: liturgical Marian texts on the Incarnation

bt67yj-k39888-d1e224.summary: Sixth argument, from patristic authority: Augustine (On Genesis Against the Manichees VIII.26) says God is interior to every thing (since all things are in him) and exterior to every thing (since he is above all and prior and posterior to all); elsewhere (Confessions I.2–3, VII.5) Augustine compares God to an infinite sea and the world to a sponge that the sea fills yet vastly exceeds on every side; Prudentius's hymn on Romanus the martyr is cited similarly ('he fills within and without and overflows').
claims: Patristic authorities (Augustine, Prudentius) describe God as both interior and exterior to the world, using the image of an infinite sea surrounding a sponge-like world, taken as support for God's existence beyond the created universe.
concepts: God as interior and exterior to creation

bt67yj-k39888-d1e260.summary: The paragraph gives the author's own resolution of the question, rejecting the imaginary-spaces view taken literally: properly speaking, God was, before the world was made, nowhere, in no place at all, because there was no place or creature whatsoever in which he could be or which he could actually contain or conserve — there was, besides God, simply nothing, and it must not be said that God is 'in nothing.' Likewise, God cannot properly be said now to be outside the world in imaginary spaces, since there is no creature outside the world and God operates nothing outside the world.
claims: Properly speaking, before creation God was nowhere and in no place, since no place or creature existed for him to be in.
It is false to say God is 'in nothing.'
Consequently, God is not now, properly speaking, in imaginary spaces outside the world, since nothing exists there and God operates nothing there.
concepts: God prior to creation as 'in nothing' denied

bt67yj-k39888-d1e287.summary: The paragraph adds that in those imaginary spaces God is present neither by essence, nor by power, nor by presence, as can easily be understood from the earlier explanation of these three modes.
claims: None of the three established modes of divine presence (essence, power, presence) applies to God's relation to merely imaginary spaces.
concepts: power/presence/essence applied negatively to imaginary spaces

bt67yj-k39888-d1e300.summary: The paragraph offers a reductio against the imaginary-spaces view: if God were in the infinite spaces of places (which do not really exist but are merely imagined by us), then by the same reasoning he would likewise be in infinite spaces of times (which neither are, nor will be, nor were), and in infinite imaginary worlds, chimeras, and whatever else the imagination can fashion — all of which are absurd.
claims: Positing God's presence in merely imagined spaces leads by parity of reasoning to absurd consequences (presence in imagined times, imagined worlds, and chimeras).

bt67yj-k39888-d1e322.summary: The paragraph notes this response is already clear from what was said above about how God is everywhere and how he is in place and time, then draws a distinction: since some imaginary things (like imaginary spaces beyond the world) could exist in reality because God is able to make and fill them, Scotus and Bonaventure and others, commenting on this distinction, rightly teach that God actually exists only in real places, but exists potentially (not actually) in imaginary places. Since what is merely potential is not simply, this is the sense in which God can be said to be, in a qualified way, in imaginary spaces and even imaginary worlds — namely, potentially.
claims: Scotus, Bonaventure, and others hold that God is actually present only in real places, and merely potentially (not actually) present in imaginary places.
Because the merely potential does not simply exist, God's 'presence' in imaginary spaces or worlds is only a potential, qualified sense of presence.

bt67yj-k39888-d1e355.summary: The paragraph cites Augustine's exposition of Psalm 122 as rightly answering the question: before creation, God was and dwelt in himself, needing no other thing in which to be or rest, as Wisdom 7 says of divine wisdom ('remaining in herself, she renews all things'), a liturgical hymn says ('unmoved, remaining in you'), and 1 Timothy 6 says of God dwelling 'in unapproachable light' — meaning God dwells in himself, since that inaccessible light is nothing other than God himself, who even now, extra omnem locum realem, remains in himself, per 1 John 1 ('God is light, and in him there is no darkness at all'); similar teachings are found in Augustine's On Faith Against the Manichaeans (ch. 37) and Nazianzen's Second Theological Oration.
claims: Before creation, God was and dwelt in himself alone, requiring nothing else in which to exist or rest.
Scriptural and patristic texts describing God as 'inaccessible light' or dwelling in himself confirm that God's mode of existence prior to and beyond creation is self-contained, not spatial.

bt67yj-k39888-d1e403.summary: Reply to the first argument: it does not follow that God is in the world definitively (as the first argument urged), because although God is not elsewhere than the world in actual fact, he could nonetheless also be elsewhere, since being of infinite power he could still make other creatures, even other worlds, beyond this world, without limit — so his non-elsewhere-ness in this world is not necessary but only a matter of fact, unlike the truly definitive presence of the soul confined to a body.
claims: God's not being 'elsewhere' than the actual world does not amount to definitive presence, because God retains the power to make other worlds or creatures beyond this one, unlike a soul necessarily confined to its body.
concepts: definitive presence distinguished from contingent non-elsewhere-ness

bt67yj-k39888-d1e423.summary: Reply to the second argument: whatever the truth of its antecedent, the argument proves nothing, because God does not have an operative power actually applied to anything outside the world (there being nothing there to which it could be applied).
claims: The second argument fails because God has no operative power actually applied outside the world, there being nothing there to apply it to.
concepts: absence of an actual object of divine operation outside the world

bt67yj-k39888-d1e435.summary: Reply to the third argument: no true motion occurs except toward a real terminus, and there is no such real terminus outside the world; even granting such a terminus, God would not be moved to it by the world's motion, not even accidentally, because he is already in it (nothing is moved toward a terminus in which it already is) — which is precisely why God is not moved even when all the things he is in are moved.
claims: True motion requires a real terminus, which does not exist outside the world.

Even granting such a terminus, God would not be moved toward it, since nothing moves toward a place it already occupies — explaining why God remains unmoved even as the things in which he exists are moved.
concepts: God's immutability amid the motion of creatures

bt67yj-k39888-d1e455.summary: Reply to the fourth argument: just as God, before all real time, existed in himself rather than in imaginary times, so too, before the world, he existed only in himself rather than in imaginary places; and just as he was in himself before the world, so he is in himself, not in any imaginary 'outside,' beyond the world.
claims: By parallel reasoning to time, God's existence 'before' and 'outside' the world is existence in himself alone, not in imaginary times or places.
concepts: parallel treatment of time and place

bt67yj-k39888-d1e471.summary: The paragraph clarifies that the expressions 'before the world' and 'outside the world' can be taken in two ways: literally, as referring to some time before the world or some place outside the world — in which sense it is false, properly speaking, that God was 'before' the world or is 'outside' it, since there was no time before the world and there is no place outside it, nor did any Father ever speak in that literal sense; or, alternatively, as signifying that God is not limited by the time or space of the world — in which sense it is true that God was before the world and is outside it, because his being and power, being uncreated and infinite, cannot be constrained or defined by those limits.
claims: 'Before the world' and 'outside the world' are ambiguous: taken literally (as designating an actual prior time or an actual exterior place) they are false of God, since no such time or place exists.
Taken as signifying non-limitation by the world's temporal and spatial bounds, these expressions are true of God, whose infinite and uncreated being cannot be constrained by such limits.
concepts: divine infinity as non-limitation rather than literal extra-spatial or extra-temporal location

bt67yj-k39888-d1e504.summary: The closing paragraph explains that the objections drawn from Scripture and the Fathers (the fifth and sixth arguments) are to be answered along these same lines: those texts signify the immensity of divine power, which is not bound to this universe or to this order of things — not a literal claim that God occupies real space beyond the world.
claims: The scriptural and patristic texts cited as objections signify the immensity of divine power, not bound to this created order, rather than asserting God's literal spatial extension beyond the world.

bt67yj-k39888.summary: Capitulum 5 poses and resolves the question of where God was before the world was created and whether he now exists in 'imaginary spaces' beyond the world. After presenting six arguments favoring a literal doctrine of divine presence in imaginary spaces (drawn from analogies with angelic presence, immutability, the priority of God to time, and scriptural/patristic transcendence language), the author rejects the literal view — properly speaking God was nowhere before creation and is nowhere outside the actual world, since no place or creature exists there for him to be in or operate on — and instead follows Augustine in holding that before and beyond creation God simply dwells in himself. Following Scotus and Bonaventure, it allows a qualified sense in which God can be said to be potentially, but not actually, present in imaginary spaces or worlds, and it systematically answers each of the six opening arguments on this basis, concluding that scriptural and patristic transcendence language signifies the immensity of divine power rather than literal extra-cosmic location.
claims: Properly speaking, God was nowhere before creation and is nowhere outside the actual world, since 'imaginary spaces' do not really exist.
God dwells 'in himself' before and beyond creation, needing no place or creature.
Following Scotus and Bonaventure, God can be said to exist only potentially, not actually, in merely imaginary spaces or worlds.
Scriptural and patristic language of God's transcendence of the cosmos signifies the immensity of his power, not literal spatial location beyond the world.
